idiom_name: stateless module mixin via include / extend
implementation_notes: Ruby's mixins are modules: `include SomeModule` inserts the module into the class's ancestor chain by reference - methods are not copied and no instance storage is added - so a module that defines only methods is a zero-storage behaviour carrier and the empty-base concern disappears. The size risk runs the other way: every instance variable a module sets (@x, or instance_variable_set) is allocated in the including object, so a 'stateless' mixin that memoises into an ivar is per-object state, and MRI grows the object's variable table when a new ivar name appears. Keep mixins stateless (derive values from other methods or from accessors supplied by the host) and document the methods the host must provide; `extend` is the per-object counterpart, useful for behaviour but not for sharing it cheaply across many objects.
code_sketch:
module Timestamped                      # no instance state of its own
  def stamp
    "#{object_id}@#{Time.now.to_i}"
  end
end

class Order
  include Timestamped                   # one ancestor entry, no per-object bytes
end

# ObjectSpace.memsize_of(Order.new) shows no storage for the mixin
pitfalls: A module that assigns @ivar creates state in every including object, and two mixins using the same ivar name silently share one variable.
include order determines the ancestor chain, so two mixins defining the same method hide one another without any warning.
extend adds the module to a single object's singleton class: great for one-off behaviour, but extending many objects costs more than a single include.
